queries: In our investigation of the neurotrophic potential of citrus by-products, we examined the effects of peel and pulp extracts from a defined panel of citrus cultivars on brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) secretion in ACHN renal adenocarcinoma cell cultures. The experimental design involved treating ACHN cells with standardized aqueous and ethanolic extracts prepared from both the flavedo/mesocarp (peel) and the juice sacs (pulp) of each selected cultivar. After a 24-hour incubation period, conditioned media were collected and BDNF concentrations were quantified using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Our results demonstrated that extracts from certain cultivars significantly upregulated BDNF levels in the culture medium, while others showed negligible or inhibitory effects. The differential response was attributed to variations in flavonoid and polymethoxyflavone profiles among the cultivars. Notably, the peel extracts generally exhibited a more pronounced effect on BDNF secretion compared to pulp extracts, likely due to higher concentrations of bioactive compounds in the outer tissues. The study included a total of ten distinct citrus cultivars, encompassing sweet oranges, mandarins, lemons, limes, and grapefruit. For each cultivar, both peel and pulp were independently processed and tested in triplicate, yielding twenty separate extract conditions. Statistical analysis using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test revealed significant differences between treatment groups. These findings suggest that citrus peel and pulp extracts hold promise as natural modulators of BDNF expression, with potential implications for neurodegenerative disease prevention. Further fractionation studies are warranted to identify the specific phytochemicals responsible for the observed bioactivity.

Summary.
Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a neurotrophin that plays fundamental roles in neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity. Its upregulation in the brain can effectively prevent and treat central nervous system (CNS) diseases, including depression, Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and Parkinson’s disease (PD). BDNF is synthesized in various peripheral tissues as well as in the brain and can be transported from peripheral circulation into the brain through the blood–brain barrier. Therefore, foods that upregulate BDNF in peripheral tissues may be beneficial in preventing and treating these CNS diseases. Previously, we revealed that treatment with Chinpi (Citrus unshiu peel) and Citrus natsudaidai increased BDNF levels in the human renal adenocarcinoma cell line ACHN. Here, we evaluated the effects of 21 citrus cultivars on BDNF production in ACHN cells by measuring BDNF levels in the cell culture medium. We found that treatment with peels and pulps of 13 citrus varieties increased BDNF levels in ACHN cells. Many citrus cultivars are consumed worldwide and used in phytotherapy for lifestyle diseases (29, 30), inflammation (31), and cancer (28, 32). However, there is insufficient information regarding the relationship between citrus cultivars and BDNF upregulation.

In this study, we analyzed the effects of the peels and pulps of 21 citrus cultivars on BDNF levels in the culture medium of ACHN cells. Furthermore, we examined the effects of some citrus cultivars on BDNF mRNA expression in ACHN cells.

Screening of citrus peel with BDNF-upregulating effect in ACHN cells.
The relative BDNF levels in the culture medium of ACHN cells treated with each citrus peel sample are shown in Fig. 1. BDNF concentrations in the control were 116.0–261.2 pg/mL. Among the 21 citrus cultivars peel, 13 showed significantly increased BDNF levels in the cell culture medium (Fig. 1). Treatment with citrus hybrids (Sweet spring and Murcott) showed a strong BDNF-upregulation effect equivalent to that of Acrumen (Fig. 1). Treatment with Osmocitrus varieties, such as Yuzu and Sudachi, but not Kabosu, resulted in 1.18- and 1.36-fold higher BDNF levels, respectively, than the control (Fig. 1). Limonellus, Citrophorum, and Cephalocitrus varieties did not elevate BDNF levels in this study (Fig. 1). BDNF concentrations in the culture medium increased depending on the number of ACHN cells (24). We, therefore, confirmed that none of the citrus peel methanol extracts that showed BDNF-upregulating activity significantly increased the viability of ACHN cells (Table 2).

Therefore, many citrus species are expected to increase peripheral BDNF levels by more than 1.3-fold in vivo, and these could be useful in the prevention and treatment of depression.

Some studies have revealed that blood BDNF levels decrease in patients with AD as well as in patients with depression (49–52). Moreover, high serum BDNF levels are related to delayed cognitive decline in patients with AD and in healthy individuals (53, 54). Patients with PD have reduced BDNF levels in the brain (13), indicating that increased levels of BDNF in the brain may contribute to the prophylaxis and treatment of PD. BDNF plays an important role in the survival of dopaminergic neurons and is involved in PD pathophysiology (55). Thus, many citrus species analyzed in this study are potential candidates for the prevention and treatment of AD and PD.

Effects of citrus cultivar peel and pulp on BDNF mRNA levels in ACHN cells.
We examined the transcript levels of BDNF mRNA in ACHN cells treated with peels and pulps of Okitsuwase, Ponkan, Clementine mandarin, and Murcott. These four citrus cultivars are consumed as edible fruits in many countries, and those BDNF-upregulating effects were potent. BDNF mRNA expression in ACHN cells treated with 100 g/mL Okitsuwase, Ponkan, Clementine mandarin, and Murcott peel was 1.68-, 1.48-, 1.44-, and 1.69-fold higher, respectively, than that in the control (Fig. 3).

In the pulp treatment group, BDNF expression in ACHN cells treated with 100 g/mL of Okitsuwase, Ponkan, Clementine mandarin, and Murcott pulp was 2.23-, 1.33-, 1.40-, and 1.67-fold higher, respectively, than that in control (Fig. 3).
